stops.name: Milan, Il Popolo d'Italia founded, expulsion from the party
stops.campa: With French subsidy and the backing of interventionist industrialists behind him, Mussolini launches Il Popolo d'Italia on 15 November, still subtitled a socialist daily out of old habit. Nine days later a howling party tribunal in Milan expels him for good; former comrades shout traitor and worse as he is driven from the hall he once commanded. He answers them, by several accounts, with a line that becomes legend: they hate him, he says, only because they still love him.
stops.quote: You hate me because you still love me.
stops.quote_source: Socialist Party expulsion tribunal, Milan, 24-25 November 1914 (widely recorded contemporary account)

stops.name: The Isonzo front, private of the Bersaglieri
stops.campa: Called up with his own class after Italy enters the war in May, Mussolini trains briefly and is sent as a private of the 11th Bersaglieri Regiment to the rock trenches of the Carso above the Isonzo. He keeps a war diary, later published, endures the winter cold, contracts paratyphoid, and is cited for steadiness under fire. The journalist who wrote for months that Italy must fight now lives, without complaint by his own account, in the mud he demanded other men enter.

stops.name: The Carso, wounded
stops.campa: Commanding a trench-mortar section, Mussolini is caught by the accidental detonation of his own unit's bombarda; more than forty fragments of shell tear into his back, legs and side, and he is carried from the line believing himself dying. Surgeons at the field hospital, working without full anesthetic, spend months extracting the metal from his body; he is discharged unfit for further combat and returns to Milan and Il Popolo d'Italia on crutches, the wound already folding itself into the legend he is building.

stops.name: Milan, Piazza San Sepolcro, the founding of the Fasci
stops.campa: In a hall of the Circolo dell'Industria e del Commercio on the Piazza San Sepolcro, before some hundred and fifty restless veterans, Arditi, futurists and revolutionary syndicalists, Mussolini founds the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento. The San Sepolcro program is a chaos of anti-plutocratic and nationalist demands, a republic invoked in one clause and the monarchy left standing in the next, unresolved and unresolvable. Within months the black-shirted squadre it spawns will say plainly, with club and petrol, what the manifesto only hints.

stops.name: Milan, watching Fiume fall
stops.campa: When Giolitti's regular army shells Gabriele d'Annunzio's occupied Fiume at Christmas to force the poet-commander out under the Treaty of Rapallo, Mussolini, who has praised the Fiume enterprise in Il Popolo d'Italia and quietly borrowed its balcony harangues, its black shirts, its Roman salute, sends no men and no guns to save it. He watches from Milan a rival cult of personality broken in five days by the very state he means one day to seize for himself, and studies the lesson without evident regret.

stops.name: Ferrara and the Po valley, the squadre
stops.campa: Across the Po valley the squadre, financed by agrarian landowners frightened of the red leagues and cooperatives, purge village after village with the manganello, forced castor oil and the torch, burning chambers of labor and party halls. At Ferrara in February the method is perfected and copied everywhere within weeks. Mussolini, still publicly for legality and a return to constitutional order, does not command each raid but rides the wave the squadristi raise, disciplining a scattered terror into the instrument that will take Rome.

stops.name: Milan, elected to the Chamber
stops.campa: After fascism's null result in the 1919 elections, Mussolini remakes tactics, running on Giolitti's National Blocs list; in the general election of May he wins a parliamentary seat from Milan, entering the very chamber his own squadristi terrorize in the streets outside. It is a double strategy, ballot alongside bludgeon, that the old liberal establishment, confident it can absorb and tame fascism through office, fails to see for what it truly is until the strategy has already succeeded.

stops.name: Rome, the Third Congress, the National Fascist Party founded
stops.campa: At the Third Fascist Congress in Rome the loose, contradictory Fasci are reorganized into the Partito Nazionale Fascista, with Mussolini installed as Duce and a program tilted now toward order, the monarchy and reconciliation with the Church rather than the old republican syndicalism of San Sepolcro. The movement trades ambiguity for discipline and street violence for party structure; the year that follows will show how much of a shaken Italy is ready to make the same trade.

stops.name: Naples, the congress and the cry of 'a Roma!'
stops.campa: At the Fascist congress in Naples, before tens of thousands of blackshirts massed in the Piazza del Plebiscito and the San Carlo theater, Mussolini all but announces the coup to come: either the government is handed to fascism, he cries, or fascism will seize it by descending on Rome. The crowd answers with the chant that gives the coming days their name. Within hours the quadrumvirate is organizing columns of squadristi from every province to converge on the capital.
stops.quote: Either they give us the government, or we will seize it by marching on Rome.
stops.quote_source: Speech at the Fascist Party congress, Naples, 24 October 1922

stops.name: Rome, the March and the appointment as prime minister
stops.campa: While some thirty thousand ill-armed squadristi camp outside a capital the regular army could easily have scattered, King Victor Emmanuel III refuses to sign Prime Minister Facta's decree of martial law. On the 29th he summons Mussolini to form a government; Mussolini travels overnight from Milan by sleeper-train and arrives the morning of the 30th in a black shirt among the frock coats of the Quirinal, sworn in as the youngest prime minister in the kingdom's history. The march itself follows him into Rome afterward, a parade of the already victorious.

stops.name: Rome, the Acerbo Law
stops.campa: With fascism holding barely a third of the Chamber, Mussolini pushes through the Acerbo Law: whichever list wins at least a quarter of the national vote takes two-thirds of the parliamentary seats outright. Liberal deputies who imagine they are taming an ambitious minister into constitutional habits vote it through. In the April 1924 election, held under a hail of squadrist intimidation, the government list duly claims its supermajority, and parliament signs away, by its own hand, the mechanism that might have checked the man it still calls prime minister.

stops.name: Rome, Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, the Matteotti kidnapping
stops.campa: Days after denouncing the fraud of the April election from the floor of the Chamber and promising documents that will prove worse, the Socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti is seized on the Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia and bundled into a waiting Lancia by five men of the Fascist Ceka. He is beaten unconscious and driven off toward the Ponte Milvio; his body will not be found for two months, buried in a shallow grave in woods outside the city. Mussolini denies all knowledge, but the killers trace back into his own inner circle.
